activities.title: What the three failures had in common
activities.source_heading: What the three failures had in common
activities.prompt_markdown:
Put your three predictions beside what happened. Then look at the pattern:

| Failure | Who spoke | What went wrong | Where the message pointed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | The shell | No program with that name | The misspelled name |
| 2 | Node.js | The file was not found | The full path it looked in |
| 3 | Node.js | The program's text breaks the grammar | A file and a line number |

The three failures are three stops on one road. Read this diagram from top to bottom. Each diamond is a question with two answers.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["You type a command and press Enter"] --> B{"Does the shell find a program with that name?"}
    B -- No --> C["The shell speaks: the name was not found. Failure 1"]
    B -- Yes --> D{"Does Node.js find the file you named?"}
    D -- No --> E["Node.js speaks: Cannot find module, and the path. Failure 2"]
    D -- Yes --> F{"Does the file follow the grammar of the language?"}
    F -- No --> G["Node.js speaks: SyntaxError, and a line number. Failure 3"]
    F -- Yes --> H["The program runs"]
```

In words: first the shell looks for a program with the name you typed. If it finds none, the shell reports it, and nothing else happens. If it finds Node.js, Node.js looks for the file you named. If the file is not there, Node.js reports the path it tried. If the file is there, Node.js checks its grammar. If the grammar is broken, Node.js reports the line. Only when all three questions are answered "yes" does the program run.

This is why "who is speaking?" comes first. It tells you how far along the road you got, and so which question failed.

In all three failures the message contained the answer, once you knew which line to read. That will not always be true. It is true far more often than a beginner expects.

activities.title: Do the test case
activities.source_heading: Do the test case
activities.prompt_markdown:
Open your ordinary browser and go to `http://127.0.0.1:4410/rooms`. Here is TC-014 again. Lesson 1's version had a precondition, "Logged in as a member". This small site has no login: everyone who opens it is treated as a member.

Run the case as you would run any case, and before step 4, **write down the total you expect to see.**

| Step | Action | Expected result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Open the Rooms page | The list of rooms is shown |
| 2 | Select the Harbour Room | The room's booking form is shown |
| 3 | Enter date 1 December 2026, start 10:00, end 12:00 | — |
| 4 | Press **Book this room** | A "Booking confirmed" message is shown |

If your browser shows times with AM and PM, the end time is 12:00 PM, noon.

You should see **Booking confirmed**, the room, the date, the time, and **Total: €0.00**.

The Harbour Room costs €12 an hour, as the Rooms page says. Two hours should cost €24.00. This site has that defect planted in it on purpose, and you have just found it the way you find defects every day: you knew what the total should be, and you looked.

Record two things before going on.

1. If you follow TC-014 exactly as written, did the case pass? Look at the expected result column.
2. Roughly how long did the four steps take you?

Now look at the terminal where the site is running. It has printed a line for each thing your browser asked for:

```text
GET /rooms
GET /rooms/harbour
POST /bookings
GET /bookings/1
```

Each line is one message from your browser to the site: three requests to *get* a page, and one that *posts*, which means sends, your booking. In Lesson 1 these were arrows in a diagram between "Browser tab" and "Booking site". Here they are real, and you can watch them arrive.

And the answer to the first question: followed exactly as written, TC-014 passed. The expected result column asks only for the message, and the message was there. That was your new colleague's first run in Lesson 1.
activities.prompt_scope: Exact authored section excerpt; may include steps and worked feedback. Read it in lesson order.

activities.title: Predict, then run the test
activities.source_heading: Predict, then run the test
activities.prompt_markdown:
Make sure the site is stopped. You pressed Ctrl+C in Section 3, and the prompt is back.

**Predict before you run.** You did TC-014 by hand and saw €0.00. The test in `tests/book-room.spec.ts` is the one from Lesson 1. Will it pass or fail? Write your prediction and one sentence of reasoning.

Now run it:

```sh
npx playwright test
```

The author's run:

```text
Running 1 test using 1 worker

  ✓  1 [chromium] › tests\book-room.spec.ts:3:1 › a member can book a free meeting room (342ms)

  1 passed (1.9s)
```

It passed. Compare that with your prediction.

Read the middle line from left to right, because you will read thousands like it.

- **`✓`** means the test passed. A failed test shows `✘`. Some terminals print `ok` and `x` instead.
- **`[chromium]`** is the name the settings file gives to this browser setup. Here it means Playwright's Chromium.
- **`tests\book-room.spec.ts:3:1`** is where the test begins: the file, then line 3, then character 1. On macOS and Linux the path is written with `/`.
- **`a member can book a free meeting room`** is the test's name, the text in quotes on that line of the file.
- **`(342ms)`** is how long the test took: about a third of a second. Your figure will differ from run to run.

The first line says `using 1 worker`: one copy of the test runner did the work. Larger suites use several at once, which a later stage teaches. The last line is the summary: `1 passed`, and the time for the whole run, which includes starting everything up.

Less than a second, against the minute or two the same four steps took you. And it passed a booking page that says a two-hour booking is free. That is the sentence from Lesson 1, no longer something you were told: **a passing test means every check that was written came out true. It does not mean the feature works.** The test checked for the heading "Booking confirmed". The heading was there.
activities.prompt_scope: Exact authored section excerpt; may include steps and worked feedback. Read it in lesson order.

activities.title: Add the check, predict, then run
activities.source_heading: Add the check, predict, then run
activities.prompt_markdown:
In Lesson 1 you read the line that would catch the €0.00 total. Now add it.

Open `tests/book-room.spec.ts`. Find the last line inside the test, the one that expects the heading. Directly under it, add this line, with the same two spaces at the start as the line above:

```ts
  await expect(page.getByText('Total: €24.00')).toBeVisible();
```

Copy it from this lesson so that every character is right, the `€` sign included. The end of the test should now read:

```ts
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Booking confirmed' })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByText('Total: €24.00')).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Save the file.** You know why from *When something goes wrong*: Playwright reads the file on the disk, not the text in the editor.

**Predict before you run:** pass or fail? If it fails, roughly how long will the test take, and which line will the report point to? Lesson 1, Section 5 has what you need.

```sh
npx playwright test
```

The author's run, with the folder path shortened:

```text
Running 1 test using 1 worker

  ✘  1 [chromium] › tests\book-room.spec.ts:3:1 › a member can book a free meeting room (5.6s)


  1) [chromium] › tests\book-room.spec.ts:3:1 › a member can book a free meeting room ──────────────

    Error: expect(locator).toBeVisible() failed

    Locator: getByText('Total: €24.00')
    Expected: visible
    Timeout: 5000ms
    Error: element(s) not found

    Call log:
      - Expect "toBeVisible" getByText('Total: €24.00') with timeout 5000ms
      - waiting for getByText('Total: €24.00')


      11 |
      12 |   await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Booking confirmed' })).toBeVisible();
    > 13 |   await expect(page.getByText('Total: €24.00')).toBeVisible();
         |                                                 ^
      14 | });
      15 |
        at C:\Users\maria\course-work\QAAE_First_Run_Kit_v1\first-run-kit\tests\book-room.spec.ts:13:49

    Error Context: test-results\book-room-a-member-can-book-a-free-meeting-room-chromium\error-context.md

  1 failed
    [chromium] › tests\book-room.spec.ts:3:1 › a member can book a free meeting room ───────────────
```

This is a long message, and you have a method for long messages. Use it.

- **Who is speaking?** Playwright Test. The `✘` line has the same shape as the `✓` line you read in Section 5.
- **What went wrong?** `expect(locator).toBeVisible() failed`. An expectation did not come true. The four lines under it say which one: the locator was `getByText('Total: €24.00')`, it was expected to be `visible`, Playwright kept trying for `5000ms`, and no such element was found.
- **Where?** The report prints the lines of the test file around the place, and marks one with `>`: line 13, the line you added.

Now connect the details to what you already know.

**The test took more than five seconds, not a third of a second.** That is the assertion's 5-second wait. Lesson 1 described it. Now you have measured it. Playwright did not look once and give up. It kept looking for the text for five seconds, in case the page was still changing, and only then failed.

**Line 12 is not marked.** The heading "Booking confirmed" was found, exactly as before. The test got all the way through the booking and failed on the one new thing you asked about.

**The message does not say "the price is wrong".** It says an element with the text "Total: €24.00" was not found. That is precisely what Playwright observed. The step from "that text was not found" to "the site charges the wrong amount" is an inference. Keep that distinction. A failure report tells you what a check observed. What it means is yours to work out.

You do not have to rely on memory to work it out. Near the end of the report, the line beginning `Error Context:` names a file, `error-context.md`, in a new folder called `test-results`. Open it from the Explorer. It begins with a few instructions addressed to an AI assistant, because the file is designed so that it can be handed to one. Below them it repeats the error. Then comes the part worth your attention: an outline, in text, of the page as it was at the moment of failure. In the author's run the outline began:

```text
- heading "Booking confirmed" [level=1]
- paragraph: "Room: Harbour Room"
- paragraph: "Date: 1 December 2026"
- paragraph: "Time: 10:00 to 12:00"
- paragraph: "Total: €0.00"
```

There is the observation that supports your inference: the page said `Total: €0.00`. The machine recorded it at the moment the check failed, without anyone taking a screenshot. In Lesson 1 this appeared as one row of a table, "the evidence can be captured automatically when a test fails". This file is the simplest form of that evidence. Later lessons work with much richer recordings.

If you ever hand that file to an AI assistant, the rules from *When something goes wrong* apply. Check what is in it before it leaves your computer. Treat the assistant's explanation as an inference to test against the outline, not as a second observation.

activities.title: Predict, then grade
activities.source_heading: Predict, then grade
activities.prompt_markdown:
Now the fault set. The grading program reports faults by **category**, and these are the six:

| Category | Faults | What the category covers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| pricing | 2 | What the customer is charged |
| booking details | 1 | Whether the confirmation describes the booking that was made |
| dates | 1 | How a date is handled or shown |
| booking flow | 1 | Whether a valid booking goes through at all |
| booking rules | 1 | What the site must allow and what it must refuse |

**Predict before you grade.** This suite checks one heading. How many of the six faults will it catch, and in which categories? Write down a number and your reasons. This prediction is the most useful one in the lesson, so take a minute over it.

Then:

```sh
npm run grade
```

It takes about half a minute. npm first prints two lines beginning with `>`, naming the command it starts. Then, in the author's run:

```text
Sample grading kit 1.0.0-draft, fault set QAAE-SAMPLE-FAULTS-1

Good build, run 1 of 3 ... passed (1 of 1 tests)
Good build, run 2 of 3 ... passed (1 of 1 tests)
Good build, run 3 of 3 ... passed (1 of 1 tests)
Fault build 1 of 6 ... missed
Fault build 2 of 6 ... missed
Fault build 3 of 6 ... missed
Fault build 4 of 6 ... missed
Fault build 5 of 6 ... caught
Fault build 6 of 6 ... missed

Good build     passed 3 of 3 runs
Fault builds   caught 1 of 6

  caught  booking flow
  missed  pricing (2 faults)
  missed  booking details
  missed  dates
  missed  booking rules

Written to results/grade-results.json
```

**One of six.** Compare that with your prediction.

Take the report apart.

- **`Good build passed 3 of 3 runs`.** No false alarm, and the same answer three times. So when this suite fails on a fault build, it is at least not something it also does on a correct site.
- **`Fault builds caught 1 of 6`.** Against five of the six faulty sites, this suite reported that everything was fine.
- **`caught booking flow`.** The one fault it caught stopped a valid booking from going through. No confirmation heading appeared, and the heading is the one thing this test looks for.
- **The four `missed` lines.** On each of those builds a customer would have been charged wrongly, or told something untrue about their booking, or allowed to do something the site should have refused. Each time the heading "Booking confirmed" appeared, and the test passed.

This is Lesson 1, with a number on it. In Lesson 1 you worked out, by reading, that this test would let the €0.00 defect through. Now you have run it against six faults and counted: it lets five through. The suite's result on the good build was "1 passed", and on five broken builds it was also "1 passed". Those passes were telling you almost nothing, and until a minute ago you had no way to see that.

activities.title: Add the price check, predict, then grade
activities.source_heading: Add the price check, predict, then grade
activities.prompt_markdown:
The report says two pricing faults were missed. You know one check for the price, from Lesson 4. Open `tests/book-room.spec.ts` and add it under the heading check, exactly as you did before:

```ts
  await expect(page.getByText('Total: €24.00')).toBeVisible();
```

Save the file.

Look at where the value `€24.00` comes from. It is the amount you calculated in Section 3: two hours at €12. It is **not** "whatever the site showed". This is the test oracle from Lesson 1 doing its work, and it is the reason you ran the case by hand and wrote your expectation down first. Only the wording, `Total:` and the form of the amount, was taken from the good build.

Suppose you had done it the other way round, and copied the whole line from the screen without asking what the amount should be. Such a check can only ever confirm that the screen shows what the screen showed that day. If the screen was wrong on the day you copied it, your test now protects the defect.

**Predict:** the report said `missed pricing (2 faults)`. You have added one check. How many of the two will it catch?

```sh
npm run grade
```

The author's run, from the summary on:

```text
Good build     passed 3 of 3 runs
Fault builds   caught 3 of 6

  caught  pricing (2 faults)
  caught  booking flow
  missed  booking details
  missed  dates
  missed  booking rules
```

Both. One line caught two faults, and you still do not know what the second pricing fault is. You do not need to know. Your check does not say "the total must not be zero". It says "the total must be €24.00". That single exact expectation is false on **every** build that gets this total wrong, whatever the cause.

That is the strength of a precise expected result. You know it from manual work, where "the correct total is shown" is a weaker expected result than "Total: €24.00". The machine makes the difference measurable.

Notice also that this run took longer than the first. A check that fails waits five seconds first, as you saw in Lesson 4. A check that passes costs almost nothing. So grading gets slower as your suite catches more. An ordinary run on a healthy product does not.
activities.prompt_scope: Exact authored section excerpt; may include steps and worked feedback. Read it in lesson order.

Carry on from row 3, one row per command, until all four of Dana's steps have run and you can explain every difference between what her note says and what you saw. There are four things to find:

1. Why the program cannot read the file in row 3, and what Dana must have had that you do not. Find two different repairs and choose one.
2. Once the check runs: your `Result` line does not match the one in Dana's note. No error is shown anywhere. Find an explanation, and design a check that supports it. Then write down what you still cannot know.
3. Why step 3 fails, and why it may have worked for Dana all the same.
4. What is wrong with the last sentence of step 4. Run the step, look at the screen, ask for the exit code, and print the file.

Finish by filling in the two sections at the end of the log: "What was wrong" and "What I am still not sure about".
activities.prompt_scope: Exact authored section excerpt; may include steps and worked feedback. Read it in lesson order.

activities.title: Practice B: rewrite the note
activities.source_heading: Practice B: rewrite the note
activities.prompt_markdown:
Write a new version of Dana's note in a file of your own, `monthly-check-revised.md`, in your `course-work` folder. A person who has the kit, on Windows, macOS or Linux, and who has never met Dana, should be able to follow it and should be able to tell whether it worked.

Before you write, list what every step of a good set of instructions needs. Then check your list against the one in the explanations.
activities.prompt_scope: Exact authored section excerpt; may include steps and worked feedback. Read it in lesson order.

activities.title: Practice C: a second note, with less help
activities.source_heading: Practice C: a second note, with less help
activities.prompt_markdown:
A different colleague, Tomas, left a different note: `handover/year-end-check.md`. Print it, read it through, and then do what you did for Dana's: follow it as written, log every command, repair one thing at a time, and get its step 4 to produce the result Tomas expects.

Then answer:

1. For each of his five steps, which row of the table in Section 2 does it break for you? The answer depends on your shell: some of his steps work as written in bash and zsh and fail in PowerShell.
2. His step 5 says the year is closed if the `Result` line is printed. In which situations is that line printed, and in which is it not? What should the step say?
3. After you have followed his note to the end, something is different about your terminal that was not different before. What is it, how could it affect the next thing you do in that terminal, and how do you put it back?
activities.prompt_scope: Exact authored section excerpt; may include steps and worked feedback. Read it in lesson order.

activities.title: Practice D: your own blind spots
activities.source_heading: Practice D: your own blind spots
activities.prompt_markdown:
You have now seen two people's notes fail. Without looking anything up:

1. Of the six rows in Section 2, which would **you** be most likely to leave out of a note, and why that one?
2. Look at your recovery note from *When something goes wrong*. Find one line in it that a stranger could not follow, and rewrite it.
3. What is the cheapest reliable way to find the gaps in instructions you have written yourself?
activities.prompt_scope: Exact authored section excerpt; may include steps and worked feedback. Read it in lesson order.
